## Likelihood

- Likelihood function describes the 'likelihood' of the parameters, $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, given the data, $X = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}$,

$$
  L(\boldsymbol{\theta}|X)
$$

- Likelihood is the same as the joint density of the data, $f$,

$$
  f(X) = f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)
$$

- Basic understanding of probability required

## Probability Mass Function

- Random variable $x$ is discrete 
- Probability mass function $f(x)$ describes probability of r.v. $x$ taking on a specific value.
- Requires that $f(x) \geq 0$ and $\sum_i f(x = i) = 1$.
- Typical Functions: Binomial, Poisson, Negative Binomial

::: {#my-long-container style="height: 200px; border: 1px solid #ccc;"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| out-width: "60%"
#| fig-align: center

x <- 0:20
fx <- dbinom(x, size = 20, prob = 0.25)
plot(x, fx, ylab = "f(x)", xlab = "x", col = "black", lwd = 3, type = "h")
sum(fx)
```
:::

## Probability Density Function

- Random variable $x$ is continuous
- Probability density function $f(x)$
- Describes a density, not a probability of an event.
- $f(x) \geq 0$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)dx = 1$ 
- Typical Functions: Normal, Student t, Gamma, Beta
- Probability defined by some area under the curve, (CDF)

$$
  p(x \leq 1) = \int_{-\infty}^1 f(x)dx
$$

::: {#my-long-container style="height: 200px; border: 1px solid #ccc;"}
```{r}
#| out-width: "60%"
#| echo: true
#| fig-align: center

x <- seq(-5, 5, by = 0.01)
fx <- dnorm(x, 0, 1)
plot(x, fx, ylab = "f(x)", xlab = "x", type = "l")
polygon(c(x[x <= 1], 1, 0), c(fx[x <= 1], 0, 0), col="blue", border=NA)
sum(fx*0.01)
```
:::

## Joint Density

- Some sample $\textbf{x}$, of size $n$
- Assume $x_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma)$ and all are independent.
- Then the joint density is
$$
\begin{aligned}
  f(\textbf{x})  & = f(x_1, \ldots, f_n)\\
  & = f(x_1)f(x_2) \cdots f(x_n)\\ 
  & =  \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i)
\end{aligned}
$$


## Example Discrete

- Draw $30$ observations from a Binomial distribution with size $20$ and probability $0.25$.
- Likelihood is 
$$
  L(p|\textbf{x}) = f(x_1) \cdots f(x_{30}).
$$

::: {#my-long-container style="height: 200px; border: 1px solid #ccc;"}
```{r}
#| out-width: "60%"
#| echo: true
#| fig-align: center

x <- rbinom(30, size = 20, prob = 0.25)
p <- seq(0, 1, 0.01)
lik <- \(p){prod(dbinom(x, prob = p, size = 20))}
likv <- Vectorize(lik)
plot(p, likv(p), type = "l", ylab = "Likelihood(p)")
```
:::


## Example Continuous

- Draw $30$ observations from a Normal distribution with mean $3$ and standard deviation $0.75$.
- Likelihood is 
$$
  L(\mu, \sigma|\textbf{x}) = f(x_1) \cdots f(x_{30}).
$$

::: {#my-long-container style="height: 400px; border: 1px solid #ccc;"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| out-width: "60%"
#| fig-align: center

x <- rnorm(30, mean = 3, sd = 0.75)
mu <- seq(2.6, 3.4, 0.1)
sigma = seq(0.4, 1.3, 0.1)
lik <- \(mu, sigma){prod(dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma))}
likv <- Vectorize(lik, vectorize.args = c("mu", "sigma"))
z <- outer(mu, sigma, likv)
filled.contour(
  x = mu, 
  y = sigma, 
  z = z,
  color.palette = terrain.colors,
  xlab = expression(mu),
  ylab = expression(sigma),
  main = "Likelihood Contour Map"
)

```
:::


## Conditional Density

- Some sample $\textbf{x}$, of size $n$
- Assume $x_i|u \sim N(u + \mu, \sigma)$
- $u \sim N(0, 1)$ is a random variable (e.g. random effect)
- The $x$ values are not independent!

$$
  f(\textbf{x}) \neq \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i)
$$
- However, conditional on the value of $u$, they are independent,

$$
  f(\textbf{x}|u) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i|u)
$$
- Joint density can be written as

$$
  f(\textbf{x}) = \int f(\textbf{x},u)du = \int f(\textbf{x}|u)f(u)du
$$

## Conditional Density

- How we write hierarchical models, for some group $j$,

\begin{align}
  x_{i} & = \mu + u_{j} + \epsilon_i \\
  u_j & \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2) \\
  \epsilon_i & \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
\end{align}

- Observations within a group $j$ are not independent.
- Conditional on the value of the random effect $u_j$ they are!

## Likelihood

- For parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta} = \{\mu, \sigma\}$
- Assuming independence between observations $x_1, \ldots, x_n$

$$
L(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \textbf{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i)
$$

- Maximum likelihood estimation -- Find maximum values of parameters given the data.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "100%"

x <- rnorm(100, 0.25, 2)
ll <- function(mu_vector) {
  sapply(mu_vector, function(m) {
    sum(dnorm(x, mean = m, sd = 2, log = TRUE))
  })
}
mu <- seq(-5, 5, 0.1)

plot(mu, ll(mu), xlab = "mu", ylab = "Log Likelihood(mu)", type = "l")

plot(mu, -ll(mu), xlab = "mu", ylab = "Negative Log-Likelihood", type = "l")
```

## Fitting a Likelihood in R

- Maximum of likelihood is also maximum of log-likelihood
- Maximization is the same as minimizing the negative.
- Multiplying small numbers is bad.
- $l(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathbf{x}) = \log(L(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathbf{x}))$


```{r, echo = TRUE}
  x <- rnorm(1000, 0, 5)
  fx <- dnorm(x, 0, 5)
  log(prod(fx))
  sum(log(fx))
```

::: {#my-long-container style="height: 400px; border: 1px solid #ccc;"}
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "100%"

x <- rnorm(100, 0.25, 2)
ll <- function(mu_vector) {
  sapply(mu_vector, function(m) {
    sum(dnorm(x, mean = m, sd = 2, log = TRUE))
  })
}
mu <- seq(-5, 5, 0.1)

plot(mu, exp(ll(mu)), xlab = "mu", ylab = "Likelihood(mu)", type = "l")

plot(mu, ll(mu), xlab = "mu", ylab = "Log-Likelihood(mu)", type = "l")
```
:::

## Fitting a Likelihood in R

- Remember that $\log(AB) = \log(A) + \log(B)$
- We build the log-likelihood by summing over the log of each independent component of the likelihood.

$$
  \log(L(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathbf{x}) = \sum \log(f(x_i)).
$$

- In R this is best done vectorized. Loops are slow, especially when nested.
- In C++ loops are very fast.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
  x <- rnorm(1000, 0, 5)
  ll_vec <- \(a){
    lfx <- dnorm(x, 0, 5, log = TRUE)
    ll <- sum(lfx)
    ll*a
  }
  ll_loop <- \(a){  
    ll <- 0
    for( i in 1:1000){
      ll <- ll + dnorm(x[i], 0, 5, log = TRUE)
    }
    ll*a
  }

  ## First taste of RTMB... :)
  ll_loopc <- RTMB::MakeTape(ll_loop, 1)
  ll_vecc <- RTMB::MakeTape(ll_vec, 1)
  
  microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
    vectorized = ll_vec(rnorm(1)),
    looped = ll_loop(rnorm(1)),
    looped_c = ll_loopc(rnorm(1)),
    vectorized_c = ll_vecc(rnorm(1)),
    times = 100
  )
```

## Likelihood in R

- Consider a sample of size 50 of $x \sim N(\mu = 2, \sigma = 5)$

```{r}
#| echo: true

x <- rnorm(50, 2, 5)

negloglik <- \(theta){
  mu <- theta[1]
  sigma <- theta[2]
  ll <- -sum(dnorm(x, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))
  return(-ll)
}
```

- Problems with this code?

## Link functions

- Optimization typically wants no discontinuities in parameter space.
- We know standard deviation is strictly positive $\sigma > 0$
- $\log$ maps a positive number to $\{\infty, \infty\}$
  * Inverse is $\exp$
- If $p \in [0,1]$, then $p/(1-p) \in [0, \infty)$
- $\alpha = \text{logit}(p) = \log(p/(1-p)) \in (-\infty, \infty)$
  * Inverse is $p = 1/(1+\exp(-\alpha))$

```{r}
#| echo: true

negloglik <- \(theta){
  mu <- theta[1]
  sigma <- exp(theta[2])
  ll <- -sum(dnorm(x, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))
  return(-ll)
}
```

## Writing a Likelihood in RTMB

```{r}
#| echo: true

library(RTMB)

negloglik <- \(theta){
  getAll(theta)
  sigma <- exp(logsigma)
  ll <- -sum(dnorm(x, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))
  return(-ll)
}

pars <- list(mu = 0, logsigma = 0)
negloglik(pars)
obj <- MakeADFun(negloglik, pars)
obj$fn(c(0,0))

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  R = negloglik(list(mu = rnorm(1), logsigma = rnorm(1))),
  RTMB = obj$fn(rnorm(2))
)
```

## Practical

- Make your sockeye Ricker model run as an `RTMB` function
- Can log productivity be any values?
- Can carrying capacity be negative?
- Note
  * `getAll` attaches list to environment.
  * Pass inputs as list of named variables
  * `MakeADFun` creates TMB object
  * Get to `obj = MakeADFun(negloglik, parameters)`
  * Run `obj$fn()`
